evidence.claim: IMF staff said Brazil's real GDP growth was 2.9% in 2022, the nonfinancial public sector primary surplus rose to 1.3% of GDP, gross debt fell to 85.9% of GDP, and the fiscal stance nevertheless turned expansionary in 2022 because of broad tax cuts on essential goods and services and higher social support.
evidence.title: Brazil: 2023 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; Staff Supplement; and Statement by the Executive Director for Brazil
evidence.excerpt: IMF staff said Brazil's real GDP growth was 2.9% in 2022, the nonfinancial public sector primary surplus rose to 1.3% of GDP, gross debt fell to 85.9% of GDP, and the fiscal stance nevertheless turned expansionary in 2022 because of broad tax cuts on essential goods and services and higher social support.
evidence.source_locator: Summary and paragraph 9 of the staff report
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Authoritative IMF country report with detailed macro and fiscal analysis for the target year.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers 2022 with retrospective analysis published in 2023.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mixed attribution: the macro outcome reflects Bolsonaro-era policy choices, commodity revenues, and independent monetary policy rather than Bolsonaro alone.
contrary_evidence: The same report credits record commodity revenues and a wage/hiring freeze for much of the fiscal improvement, so not all positive movement is attributable to Bolsonaro.

evidence.claim: IBGE reported that Brazil's IPCA ended 2022 at 5.79%, down from 10.06% in 2021.
evidence.title: IPCA vai a 0,62% em dezembro e fecha 2022 em 5,79%
evidence.excerpt: IBGE reported that Brazil's IPCA ended 2022 at 5.79%, down from 10.06% in 2021.
evidence.source_locator: Opening summary and table of annual results
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary national statistics release for the consumer price index.
evidence.ruler_attribution: National outcome under Bolsonaro's last year in office, but heavily affected by external price shocks and monetary policy beyond his direct control.
contrary_evidence: Inflation improved versus 2021, so 2022 was not a straight-line deterioration.

evidence.claim: IBGE reported an average annual unemployment rate of 9.3% in 2022, an average employed population of 98.0 million, and average labor underutilization of 20.8%.
evidence.title: Continuous PNAD: in 2022, average annual unemployment rate was 9.3%, average annual underutilization rate was 20.8%
evidence.excerpt: IBGE reported an average annual unemployment rate of 9.3% in 2022, an average employed population of 98.0 million, and average labor underutilization of 20.8%.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary national labor-market statistics release for 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly context and outcome: labor recovery occurred under Bolsonaro but was also shaped by the pandemic rebound and macro conditions.
contrary_evidence: The level remained high by historical standards, so the recovery was partial rather than decisive.

evidence.claim: IBGE said average real monthly household income per capita reached R$1,586 in 2022, up 6.9% from 2021, the Auxílio Brasil/Bolsa Família beneficiary share in households rose to 16.9%, and the Gini index for household income per capita fell to 0.518, the lowest in the series.
evidence.title: In 2022, labor market and "Auxílio Brasil" cash transfer program allow income recovery
evidence.excerpt: IBGE said average real monthly household income per capita reached R$1,586 in 2022, up 6.9% from 2021, the Auxílio Brasil/Bolsa Família beneficiary share in households rose to 16.9%, and the Gini index for household income per capita fell to 0.518, the lowest in the series.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary statistics release with explicit 2022 income and inequality estimates.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mixed: the income recovery reflects labor-market rebound and social-transfer policy under Bolsonaro's administration, not Bolsonaro alone.
contrary_evidence: The article itself notes that benefit-category shifts may partly reflect respondent confusion and migration between programs.

evidence.claim: IBGE reported Brazil's nominal monthly household income per capita at R$1,625 in 2022, ranging from R$814 in Maranhão to R$2,913 in the Federal District.
evidence.title: IBGE releases per capita household earnings 2022 for Brazil and Federation Units
evidence.excerpt: IBGE reported Brazil's nominal monthly household income per capita at R$1,625 in 2022, ranging from R$814 in Maranhão to R$2,913 in the Federal District.
evidence.source_locator: Summary table for Brazil and federation units
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary national statistics release with state-level 2022 values.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly inherited and structural, though it sets the baseline for assessing Bolsonaro-era distributional performance.
contrary_evidence: The measure is descriptive rather than causal, so it cannot on its own prove presidential responsibility for regional gaps.

evidence.claim: IBGE reported that poverty in Brazil stood at 31.6% in 2022 and extreme poverty at 5.9%, before both rates fell in 2023.
evidence.title: In 2023, poverty in the country drops to lowest level since 2012
evidence.excerpt: IBGE reported that poverty in Brazil stood at 31.6% in 2022 and extreme poverty at 5.9%, before both rates fell in 2023.
evidence.source_locator: Highlights section and poverty summary paragraphs
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary statistical release that provides the 2022 baseline and 2023 comparison.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective but directly states the 2022 target-year baseline.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Contextual baseline for Bolsonaro's last year; the later improvement does not itself prove 2022 policy causation.
contrary_evidence: Because the article is retrospective, it is better for baseline and trajectory than for sharp attribution.

evidence.claim: The amendment recognized a 2022 state of emergency from fuel-price spikes and expanded Auxílio Brasil by R$200 per month from August to December 2022, while authorizing fuel-tax relief and transport aid.
evidence.title: Emenda Constitucional nº 123
evidence.excerpt: The amendment recognized a 2022 state of emergency from fuel-price spikes and expanded Auxílio Brasil by R$200 per month from August to December 2022, while authorizing fuel-tax relief and transport aid.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary constitutional amendment with explicit benefit and tax-relief provisions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Enacted during Bolsonaro's presidency and implemented by his administration, though the legislative coalition and Congress drove the measure.
contrary_evidence: This is short-term relief policy; it does not prove durable productivity gains or fiscal sustainability.

evidence.claim: The ministry advanced the August 2022 payment schedule and said the program's minimum benefit would be R$600 starting August 9 under PEC 1/22.
evidence.title: Ministério da Cidadania antecipa calendário do Auxílio Brasil em agosto
evidence.excerpt: The ministry advanced the August 2022 payment schedule and said the program's minimum benefit would be R$600 starting August 9 under PEC 1/22.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous government implementation notice for the cash-transfer increase.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Bolsonaro's administration as the implementing executive authority.
contrary_evidence: The increase was temporary and tied to the election-year emergency package.

evidence.claim: The government dismissed the IPEA president and named Erik Figueiredo, then the Economy Ministry's subsecretary of fiscal policy, as his replacement to make the institute more propositive.
evidence.title: Governo exonera presidente do Ipea e nomeia auxiliar de Guedes como substituto
evidence.excerpt: The government dismissed the IPEA president and named Erik Figueiredo, then the Economy Ministry's subsecretary of fiscal policy, as his replacement to make the institute more propositive.
evidence.source_locator: Lead paragraphs and the description of Figueiredo's prior role
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting through a major Brazilian outlet on a concrete appointment inside the economic policy apparatus.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Bolsonaro-administration appointment, but the evidence is about staffing rather than economic outcomes.
contrary_evidence: A technocratic appointment is only weak evidence of competence unless paired with results.

evidence.claim: Bolsonaro said he intended to change the spending cap after the October election to make room for higher infrastructure spending.
evidence.title: Brazil's Bolsonaro vows to change spending cap rule after election
evidence.excerpt: Bolsonaro said he intended to change the spending cap after the October election to make room for higher infrastructure spending.
evidence.source_locator: Lead paragraphs and direct quote in the article
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting with a direct Bolsonaro quote and clear policy context.
contrary_evidence: The proposal was deferred until after the election, which makes the motive look partly electoral rather than technocratic.

evidence.claim: Brazil's government lowered its 2022 primary deficit forecast because of booming tax collection, but also froze R$6.739 billion in spending to comply with the spending cap.
evidence.title: Brazil government improves primary budget deficit forecast for 2022
evidence.excerpt: Brazil's government lowered its 2022 primary deficit forecast because of booming tax collection, but also froze R$6.739 billion in spending to comply with the spending cap.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on official fiscal figures and the spending-freeze response.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mixed: revenue windfalls were external, while the spending freeze was a policy response by Bolsonaro's government.
contrary_evidence: The improved fiscal outlook was helped by record tax and royalty revenues, so it was not purely a policy success.

evidence.claim: The government planned to veto R$3.1 billion in budget items to fund payroll, while leaving the electoral fund at R$4.9 billion, a politically difficult choice in an election year.
evidence.title: Brazil government to veto 3.1 billion reais in budget items to fund payroll -sources
evidence.excerpt: The government planned to veto R$3.1 billion in budget items to fund payroll, while leaving the electoral fund at R$4.9 billion, a politically difficult choice in an election year.
evidence.source_locator: Lead paragraph and the section on the electoral fund and payroll allocations
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting based on Ministry of Economy sources and the official budget process.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Bolsonaro administration budget choice, but shaped by Congress and election-year politics.
contrary_evidence: The decision was partly constrained by Congress already having approved the budget bill.
